props.title: Troll 2

sections.content: Troll 2 (1990) stands as perhaps the most fascinating "best-worst movie" ever made, surpassing even Plan 9 from Outer Space (1959) in its spectacular incompetence. Italian director Claudio Fragasso, working under the pseudonym Drake Floyd, created an accidental masterpiece of failure that has nothing to do with the original Troll (1986). The film follows a family terrorized by vegetarian goblins (not trolls) who turn people into plants before eating them. The infamous "Oh my God!" scene with Michael Stephenson has become a legendary moment in cult cinema, while Deborah Reed's unhinged performance as Creedence Leonore Gielgud delivers some of the most memorably bizarre acting ever captured on film.

sections.content: The "so bad it's good" phenomenon gained mainstream recognition through films like The Room (2003) and Birdemic: Shock and Terror (2010), but Troll 2 remains unique in how every aspect of filmmaking fails spectacularly yet cohesively. The awkward dialogue (written by Italian screenwriters with limited English), the bargain-basement goblin masks, and the baffling plot about vegetarian monsters serving green-colored ice cream all combine into something transcendently entertaining. The film's journey from obscurity to cult status is documented in Best Worst Movie (2009), directed by former child star Michael Stephenson. SUBHEAD: The Art of Accidental Cinema

What separates Troll 2 from mere bad movies is its absolute sincerity. Unlike intentionally campy films like Sharknado (2013), Fragasso genuinely believed he was making a serious horror film about American family values. This earnestness places it alongside films like Manos: The Hands of Fate (1966) and Miami Connection (1987) in the pantheon of sincere failures that become unintentional comedies. The film's popularity sparked a revolution in how we view and celebrate bad cinema, leading to regular midnight screenings and fan events that rival The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975).
